title: Quality and Authenticity Evaluation of Condiments Using Near-Infrared Spectroscopy: A Critical Review
content: Condiment matrices are chemically complex, and seasonings of different categories suffer from batch-to-batch variations and high risks of adulteration. Conventional physicochemical titration and chromatographic methods involved laborious sample pretreatment and long assay durations, which hindered their applications for on-line production monitoring and large-scale commodity screening. Combined with chemometrics, near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) had enabled rapid, non-destructive and simultaneous multi-parameter analysis, and had emerged as a vital tool for condiment quality assessment. This review had systematically summarized research advances of NIRS in condiment analysis, covering quantitative determination of physicochemical properties, authentication and adulteration detection, geographical origin tracing, and on-line monitoring of fermentation processes. Key bottlenecks restricting industrial implementation had been discussed, including spectral overlap interferences derived from complex matrices, limited sensitivity toward trace constituents, poor model transferability across instruments, and the absence of unified industrial standards and shared spectral libraries. Prospects had been proposed from the perspectives of multi-modal data fusion, spectral interpretation algorithms, full-supply-chain quality traceability, and standardization, providing theoretical support and references for the technical upgrading and large-scale industrial implementation of rapid condiment detection.
